name: Adam Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both the public version and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, happy to. I work at a mid-size supermarket in the city centre, the kind with twelve aisles and a big online-orders room out the back. I'm on the tills in the morning rush, then from about eleven I run the click-and-collect desk, where people pick up the shopping they ordered on the app. I've been there six years, so I'm the one they call when the scanners or the label printer play up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy fixing things, honestly more than serving. Last year I used an AI chat tool to build a spreadsheet that tells us which yoghurts and salads to mark down at what time, and waste on chilled dropped by about a fifth. What drains me is the Saturday queue when the app double-books collection slots, and I've got eight people glaring at me and a printer jammed with labels. I share a flat with my mate Theo, and on my days off I fix old phones and sell them online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because I use these tools every day and they're handy but they're not magic. At work I'd say the self-checkouts and the app are the real changes, and they happened already. Online I'd probably post a meme about the robot apocalypse that never turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's pretty good for me. I'm the person who makes the small tools work, and in this picture small tools are all there is. My pay's normal, I've got about four months in the bank, and there are three other supermarkets within a mile that would take me tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push to get the markdown spreadsheet used across the whole region, because my manager said head office liked it. I'd ask for a pay bump for that, because I'm doing an office job on a till wage. And I'd keep the phone repairs going, which bring in about a hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually. A bit bored maybe, if nothing big ever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're doing an office job on a till wage. Would you really ask for more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, but carefully. I'd show the waste numbers, the fifth less thrown away, and ask for a small title like systems champion with an extra pound an hour. If they say no, I'd still keep doing it, because it's the part of the job I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mostly. Theo and I got a letter saying it's going up again in March, so that's sixty more each. It's annoying, not scary, because the phone money covers it.

say: AI tools are **handy but not magic**; I use them every day.
The **self-checkouts and the app** were the real changes, and they've already happened.
think: Small tools suit him, because he's the person who **makes them work** in the store.
Normal pay, **four months saved** and three other supermarkets nearby make him feel secure.
do: Push to get his **markdown spreadsheet** used across the region.
Ask for a **systems champion** title and an extra pound an hour.
Keep **phone repairs** going for about a hundred and fifty a month.
feel: **Fine**, maybe a little bored if nothing big happens.
S0.quote: I'm doing an office job on a till wage.
fieldNote: Already uses AI daily and has a **concrete result**: chilled waste down about a fifth.
Feels **secure** because of savings, local options and his fixer role.
Only pressure named is a **rent rise** in March, covered by side income.

steps.text: Pitch the markdown spreadsheet to head office for the whole region
Keep running the click-and-collect desk and ask for a pay bump
Keep fixing and selling old phones on days off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be the person who likes the new stuff. At work I'd tell people not to fight it, learn it, because the ordering and the rota are going to be done by software anyway. Online I'd probably be a bit annoying about it, posting what tools I'm using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the till part of my job is on borrowed time, but the part where I keep the machines and the app running grows for a while. The risk is that head office buys a system that does what my spreadsheet does, and then I'm just a cashier again. So I'd want to move before that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd apply for the store systems coordinator job that comes up now and then, the person who looks after the tills, scanners and app for five stores. I'd do a short online course in IT support, the kind with a certificate, about three months of evenings. And I'd start using the AI tools for ordering on purpose, so I'm the one who knows them when they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of excited, a little nervous. It's like when the app launched, everyone moaned and I learned it in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move before head office replaces you. How would you know when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When people from the regional office start watching how we do the orders with clipboards, that's the sign to move. They did that before the self-checkouts too, two people with clipboards for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor Joyce, who's brilliant with people but hates screens. If the job becomes looking after software, she's in trouble, and she's got a teenager. I'd probably try to teach her the basics, but I don't know if she'd want me to.

say: It's a good time to **like the new stuff**; don't fight it, learn it.
The **ordering and rota** will be done by software anyway, so I'd tell colleagues to get ahead.
think: The **till part** of his job is on borrowed time.
Head office could buy a system that copies his spreadsheet and make him **just a cashier** again.
do: Apply for the **store systems coordinator** role covering five stores.
Do a three-month evening **IT support course** with a certificate.
Use AI **ordering tools** on purpose so he knows them first.
feel: **Excited** with a little nervousness, like when the app launched.
S1.quote: When people from the regional office start watching how we do the orders with clipboards, that's the sign to move.
fieldNote: Reads **warning signs** from experience: clipboards came before the self-checkouts too.
Believes his own income is fairly safe if he **moves early** into systems work.
Shows care for a less technical **supervisor**, Joyce, without overpromising.

steps.text: Apply for the five-store systems coordinator job
Finish a three-month evening IT support certificate
Practise the new AI ordering tools before they roll out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and I'd say people should get ready now, not next year. At work I'd probably be the one explaining what AGI means in the canteen. Online I'd share stuff, but honestly I'd be careful, because nobody likes the guy who says I saw it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit. If AI can do almost any thinking work by 2028, then my systems plan is gone, because the AI can fix the app better than me. What's left is hands-on, and robots come about 2031, so I've got three years where my hands still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch to something physical with machines, like training as a field technician for the robots and self-checkouts, because someone has to install and repair them in that first wave. I'd stop the phone repairs, the AI can diagnose those, and put that time into the training. I'd also push my savings from four months to eight by cutting takeaways and the gym, about two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. For the first time picturing this, I'm not sure I'd be ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robot repairs, but robots might repair robots. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I have, and it's the bit I can't answer. I think for a few years after 2031 there'd be loads of them breaking in weird ways in old buildings with sticky floors. That's my window, maybe five or six years of good money, and I'd save hard during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to stop renewing the lease for a year at a time and go month to month. He works in a call centre, so he's more exposed than me, and he'd be gone in the first wave. We'd probably end up needing a cheaper place together, further out.

say: It's **huge**, and people should get ready now, not next year.
I'd explain **what AGI means** in the canteen but avoid sounding smug.
think: AGI by 2028 kills his **systems plan**, because AI could fix the app better than him.
He has about **three years** where his hands still matter before robots arrive.
do: Train as a **field technician** for robots and self-checkouts.
Drop phone repairs and grow savings from four to **eight months**.
Cut takeaways and the gym, about **two hundred** a month.
feel: **Anxious**, unsure for the first time that he'd stay ahead.
S2.quote: For the first time picturing this, I'm not sure I'd be ahead of it.
fieldNote: The adaptive optimist **wobbles** here; his thinking-work route is closed first.
Clear grasp of the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots.
Plans to bank a **short window** of repair work rather than a career.
Also worried for flatmate Theo in a **call centre**, which could raise his own rent.

steps.text: Enrol on a field technician course for self-checkouts and store robots
Cut takeaways and the gym to save two hundred more a month
Move with Theo to a cheaper month-to-month flat further out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you start now. At work I'd tell the younger lads on nights to use the time, not panic. Online I'd post the courses I'm doing, because that's what helped me with the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three is eight years before my hands are replaceable, and that's a career length for some jobs. My systems plan works for maybe three or four of those years, then I switch to the hands-on side. It feels like a ladder I can actually see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the systems coordinator job and the IT certificate. By year three I'd move into installing the robots and self-checkouts for the company that supplies us, because they'll be hiring hard. I'd put a bit of the extra pay into a simple index fund, maybe a hundred a month, just so something keeps growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady, a bit restless. I like having a plan with dates on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the bit of the plan most likely to go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting the supplier job. They might only hire engineers with proper qualifications, not a guy who fixed scanners in a supermarket. So I'd ask their technician, the one who comes every month, what they actually look for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd invest. Why now rather than just saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if these companies win, I want a tiny slice of it rather than nothing. I'm not betting the rent. It's a hundred a month I'd otherwise spend on games.

say: **Five years** is enough if you start now.
I'd post **the courses** I'm doing, because sharing helped with the app.
think: Five years plus three gives about **eight years** before his hands are replaceable.
The plan feels like a **ladder he can see**: systems work first, then installation.
do: Get the **systems coordinator** job and the IT certificate in year one.
Move to the **supplier's installation team** by year three.
Put about **a hundred a month** into an index fund.
feel: **Steady** and a bit restless, glad to have a plan with dates.
S3.quote: Five years plus three is eight years before my hands are replaceable, and that's a career length for some jobs.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn fear into a **staged plan**.
Honest about the weak link: the supplier may want **formal qualifications**.
Small **investing** move framed as owning a slice, not a gamble.

steps.text: Take the systems coordinator job and IT certificate in year one
Ask the supplier's visiting technician what installers need to qualify
Put a hundred a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, use it. At work I'd say most of us will be fine if we learn one new thing a year. Online I'd probably not say much, ten years doesn't get clicks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years plus three for robots takes me to forty. I'd have time to get properly qualified, maybe even an engineering diploma part-time. The only thing that bothers me is that ten years makes people lazy, me included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the supermarket for now, get the systems role, then start a two-year part-time engineering diploma around year three. I'd keep the index fund going and keep my four months of savings. I'd also teach Joyce and anyone else who wants it how to use the tools, because I'd rather the store kept its people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like normal life with a big deadline far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years makes people lazy. How would you stop that in yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the diploma start date in my calendar for 2029 and tell everyone, because that's how I quit smoking. Theo would nag me for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do the phone repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for a few years, because it's fun and it's money. By the mid-2030s I'd guess people just send their phone back and a machine fixes it. I'd stop when it stops paying.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, so use it.
Most of us will be fine if we **learn one new thing** a year.
think: Ten years plus three takes him to **forty**, with time to get properly qualified.
His one worry is that a long warning makes people **lazy**, himself included.
do: Get the systems role, then start a part-time **engineering diploma** around 2029.
Keep the **index fund** and four months' savings.
Teach Joyce and others to **use the tools**.
feel: **Calm**, like normal life with a big deadline far off.
S4.quote: I'd put the diploma start date in my calendar for 2029 and tell everyone, because that's how I quit smoking.
fieldNote: A long warning suits an **adaptive** person with savings; he sees a full career change.
Uses a **public commitment** trick, as when he quit smoking.
Wants the store to **keep its people**, not only himself.

steps.text: Start a two-year part-time engineering diploma in 2029
Keep the index fund going at a hundred a month
Keep working at the supermarket while moving into the systems role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it's the one where my thinking-work plan dies and I'm racing the robots with three years' notice. What would help is cheap, fast technician courses that employers actually recognise, and the supermarket giving staff paid hours to train instead of making us do it at midnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. A lot of people at the click-and-collect desk are lonely, and the chat at the desk is the only conversation some of them get all day. A robot can hand over the bags, but I'm not sure anyone's counting what goes missing when it does.

headlineQuote: A robot can hand over the bags, but I'm not sure anyone's counting what goes missing when it does.
portrait: Adam, 27, runs the **click-and-collect desk** at a city supermarket and shares a flat with his friend Theo.
He uses AI daily and built a **markdown spreadsheet** that cut chilled waste by about a fifth.
He reads the shift towards **systems work** as his chance, and plans to move before head office replaces him.
AGI by 2028 shakes him, closing his **thinking-work route** and leaving only three hands-on years.
With longer warning he builds a calm **staged plan** towards robot installation and an engineering diploma.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his systems plan dies and he races robots with three years' notice.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid hours** to train at work, not at midnight.
